imo-2024-01.title: Shift by $2$, then a small counterexample
imo-2024-01.body:
Let $S_n(\alpha)=\lfloor\alpha\rfloor+\dots+\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$.

**Even integers work:** if $\alpha=2t$, then $S_n(\alpha)=2t(1+\dots+n)=n(n+1)t$.

**Shifting.** $S_n(\alpha+2)=S_n(\alpha)+2(1+\dots+n)=S_n(\alpha)+n(n+1)\equiv S_n(\alpha)\pmod n$. So $\alpha$ has the property iff $\alpha+2$ does, and we may assume $-1\le\alpha<1$.

- $\alpha=0$ works (it is even).
- $\alpha=-1$ (so originally an odd integer): $S_2=-1-2=-3$ is not divisible by $2$.
- $0<\alpha<1$: let $m\ge2$ be the least integer with $m\alpha\ge1$. For $i<m$, $0<i\alpha<1$, and $m\alpha=(m-1)\alpha+\alpha<2$. So $S_m=0+\dots+0+1=1$, not divisible by $m$.
- $-1<\alpha<0$: let $m\ge2$ be the least integer with $m\alpha<-1$. For $i<m$, $-1\le i\alpha<0$, so $\lfloor i\alpha\rfloor=-1$; and $m\alpha\ge-1+\alpha>-2$, so $\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor=-2$. Thus $S_m=-(m-1)-2=-(m+1)$, not divisible by $m$.

**Answer:** $\alpha$ must be an even integer.

imo-2024-02.title: Use the modulus $ab+1$
imo-2024-02.body:
**$(1,1)$ works:** the gcd is always $\gcd(2,2)=2$.

Conversely, suppose $x_n=\gcd(a^n+b,b^n+a)$ equals $g$ for all $n\ge N$. Let $M=ab+1$; then $\gcd(a,M)=\gcd(b,M)=1$, so by Euler's theorem $a^{\varphi(M)}\equiv b^{\varphi(M)}\equiv1\pmod M$. Choose $n$ to be a multiple of $\varphi(M)$ with $n-1\ge N$; then $x_{n-1}=x_n=x_{n+1}=g$, and $a^n\equiv b^n\equiv1\pmod M$.

- **$n-1$:** $a(a^{n-1}+b)=a^n+ab\equiv1+(-1)=0\pmod M$, and $a$ is invertible mod $M$, so $M\mid a^{n-1}+b$. Likewise $M\mid b^{n-1}+a$. Hence $M\mid x_{n-1}=g$.
- **$n$:** now $M\mid x_n$, so $M\mid a^n+b\equiv1+b$ and $M\mid b^n+a\equiv 1+a$. Thus $a\equiv b\equiv-1\pmod M$.
- **$n+1$:** $M\mid x_{n+1}$, so $M\mid a^{n+1}+b\equiv a+b\equiv-2\pmod M$.

So $ab+1=M\mid 2$, which forces $a=b=1$.

**Answer:** $(a,b)=(1,1)$.

imo-2024-03.title: Small and big numbers, then a finite automaton
imo-2024-03.body:
Note: for every $m>N$, $a_m=x$ means that $a_{m-1}$ was then making its $x$-th appearance; in particular, if a value $v$ makes its $i$-th appearance at an index $\ge N$, the next term is $i$. Let $M>\max(a_1,\dots,a_N)$; any value $\ge M$ only occurs at indices $>N$.

**1. Some value occurs infinitely often.** Otherwise arbitrarily large values occur; the first appearance of each value $x\ge M$ is followed by $1$, so $1$ occurs infinitely often.

**2. Each value $x\ge M$ occurs at most $M-1$ times.** Otherwise take the first index $n$ at which some $x\ge M$ makes its $M$-th appearance. Its $M$ appearances are preceded by $M$ terms each making its $x$-th appearance; these are $M$ *distinct* values, each having appeared at least $x\ge M$ times before index $n$. At most $M-1$ of them are less than $M$, so some value $\ge M$ made its $M$-th appearance before $n$ — contradicting minimality.

**3. Small, medium, big.** By 1 and 2 the values occurring infinitely often are finitely many; let $k$ be the largest. Since $k$ occurs infinitely often, infinitely many values $>M$ occur at least $k$ times, and their $1$st, ..., $k$-th appearances are followed by $1,\dots,k$: so **each of $1,\dots,k$ occurs infinitely often**. Only finitely many values occur more than $k$ times (otherwise $k+1$ would occur infinitely often by the same argument); let $l\ge k$ be at least the largest of them. Call $x$ *small* if $x\le k$, *medium* if $k<x\le l$, *big* if $x>l$. Small values occur infinitely often, medium values finitely often, big values at most $k$ times each.

Choose $N'>N$ with $a_{N'}$ small such that by index $N'$ all medium values have made all their appearances and every small value has appeared more than $\max(k,N)$ times. For $n\ge N'$: if $a_n$ is small, then $a_{n+1}>\max(k,N)$ and is not medium, so it is big; if $a_n$ is big, it occurs at most $k$ times, so $a_{n+1}\le k$ is small. Thus **from $N'$ on the terms alternate small, big, small, big, ...**, and the small terms are $a_{N'},a_{N'+2},\dots$, i.e. a tail of one of the two subsequences in the problem. Also every big term after $N'$ is $>\max(k,N)$.

**4. What follows a big term.** Let $n>N'$, $a_n=g$ big, $a_{n+1}=h$. Every small value eventually makes its $g$-th appearance, at an index $\ge g>N$, and that appearance is followed by $g$. This already gives $k$ appearances of $g$, and $g$ appears at most $k$ times, so these are *all* the appearances of $g$. Hence the $h$-th appearance of $g$ follows the $h$-th small value (in time) to reach $g$ appearances, i.e.
$$h=\#\{\text{small values that have appeared at least }g\text{ times in }a_1,\dots,a_n\}.$$

**5. The automaton.** For $n\ge N'$ with $a_n$ small, let $b_i$ ($1\le i\le k$) be the number of appearances of $i$ in $a_1,\dots,a_n$, and $j=a_n$. Then $a_{n+1}=b_j$, and by step 4
$$a_{n+2}=\#\{i:\ b_i\ge b_j\}.$$
Then $b_{a_{n+2}}$ increases by $1$ and $j$ becomes $a_{n+2}$. So the *state* $(b_1,\dots,b_k;\,j)$ evolves deterministically, and the rule only uses comparisons between the $b_i$; hence the *reduced state* $(b_2-b_1,\dots,b_k-b_1;\,j)$ also evolves deterministically. If the differences $b_i-b_1$ stay bounded, there are finitely many reduced states, so the reduced state, and with it $j=a_{N'+2t}$, is eventually periodic, which proves the problem. It remains to bound the differences.

**6. Upper bound: $b_{i+1}\le b_i+C$ for a constant $C$.** Map each appearance of $i+1$ at an index $m>N$ whose predecessor $a_{m-1}=v$ is $\ge M$ to the term following the $i$-th appearance of $v$ (which is an $i$, occurring earlier). This map is injective. Appearances of $i+1$ not covered are those at indices $\le N$ or with predecessor $v<M$ (each such $v$ makes its $(i+1)$-st appearance once), so at most $N+M$. Thus $b_{i+1}\le b_i+C$ with $C=N+M$, at all times.

**7. Lower bound.** Suppose $b_{r+1}-b_r$ were unbounded below for some $r<k$. It changes by at most $1$ per step, so at some step (after $N'$) $b_r$ has just been increased (so $j=r$) and $b_{r+1}-b_r<-(k-1)C$. For $i\le r<i'$, using step 6,
$$b_i-b_{i'}\ge(b_r-(r-i)C)-(b_{r+1}+(i'-r-1)C)>(k-1)C-(k-2)C\ge0,$$
so $\min(b_1,\dots,b_r)>\max(b_{r+1},\dots,b_k)$. Now if $j\le r$, then every $i$ with $b_i\ge b_j$ satisfies $i\le r$, so the next active value $\#\{i:b_i\ge b_j\}$ is at most $r$, and only one of $b_1,\dots,b_r$ grows, preserving the inequality. By induction only $b_1,\dots,b_r$ grow from now on, so $b_k$ stays fixed — but $k$ occurs infinitely often. Contradiction.

Hence each $b_{i+1}-b_i$ is bounded above and below, all $b_i-b_1$ are bounded, and by step 5 the small terms, which form a tail of $a_1,a_3,\dots$ or of $a_2,a_4,\dots$, are eventually periodic. ∎

imo-2024-04.title: Reflect $A$ in $I$
imo-2024-04.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$. Let $T$ be the reflection of $A$ in $I$; note $T$ lies on line $AIP$.

**Removing $K$ and $L$.** The homothety with centre $A$ and ratio $2$ maps $K,I,L$ to $C,T,B$, so $\angle KIL=\angle CTB$.

**The tangent lines pass through $T$.** The tangent to $\omega$ parallel to $AC$ (other than $AC$) is the reflection of line $AC$ in $I$, so it passes through $T$; hence $XT\parallel AC$. Similarly $YT\parallel AB$.

**Two cyclic quadrilaterals.** Since $YT\parallel AB$ and $A,T,P$ are collinear,
$$\measuredangle TYC=\measuredangle ABC=\measuredangle APC=\measuredangle TPC,$$
so $C,Y,P,T$ are concyclic. In the same way $\measuredangle TXB=\measuredangle ACB=\measuredangle APB=\measuredangle TPB$, so $B,X,P,T$ are concyclic.

**Angle chase.** Using these circles and the collinearity of $B,X,Y,C$:
$$\measuredangle CTB=\measuredangle CTP+\measuredangle PTB=\measuredangle CYP+\measuredangle PXB=\measuredangle XYP+\measuredangle PXY=-\measuredangle YPX=\measuredangle XPY.$$

**Converting to ordinary angles.** Let $a,b,c,s$ be the sides and semiperimeter, $r$ the inradius, $\Delta$ the area. The line $XT$ is at distance $2r$ from $AC$, so $CX=a\cdot\frac{2r}{h_b}=\frac{ab}{s}$; similarly $BY=\frac{ac}{s}$. Since $b,c<s$ and $BX=a-\frac{ab}s<\frac{ac}{s}=BY$ (equivalent to $a<b+c$), the points lie in the order $B,X,Y,C$. Also $T$ is at signed distance $2r-h_a$ from $BC$ and $2r<h_a\iff a<b+c$, so $T$, like $P$, lies on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$. Seen from $T$ and from $P$ (same side of $BC$), the rotations from $TB$ to $TC$ and from $PX$ to $PY$ have the same sense; so $\measuredangle CTB=\measuredangle XPY$ means $\angle CTB\equiv-\angle XPY\pmod{180^\circ}$. Both angles lie strictly between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, hence
$$\angle KIL+\angle YPX=\angle CTB+\angle XPY=180^\circ.$$
∎

imo-2024-05.title: Two attempts can fail; a three-attempt strategy
imo-2024-05.body:
Write $(r,c)$ for the cell in row $r$ and column $c$.

**Two attempts are not enough.** On the first attempt, the first cell of row $2$ that Turbo enters, say $(2,i)$, may contain a monster; then he learns nothing beyond row $1$. On the second attempt, the first cell of row $3$ he enters is $(3,j)$, reached from $(2,j)$, so $j\ne i$; that cell may hold row $3$'s monster (it is in a different column from the monster at $(2,i)$). So Turbo can fail twice.

**Three attempts suffice.** *Attempt 1:* walk $(1,1)\to(2,1)\to(2,2)\to\dots\to(2,2023)$. This meets row $2$'s monster, say at $(2,i)$. Column $i$ then contains no other monster, and row $2$ is otherwise safe.

*Case $2\le i\le2022$.* Try the two paths
$$(1,i-1)\to(2,i-1)\to(3,i-1)\to(3,i)\to(4,i)\to\dots\to(2024,i),$$
$$(1,i+1)\to(2,i+1)\to(3,i+1)\to(3,i)\to(4,i)\to\dots\to(2024,i).$$
The only cells that might hold monsters are $(3,i-1)$ and $(3,i+1)$, and row $3$ has only one monster, so one of the two attempts succeeds.

*Case $i=1$ (the case $i=2023$ is symmetric).* *Attempt 2:* follow the staircase
$$(1,2)\to(2,2)\to(2,3)\to(3,3)\to(3,4)\to\dots\to(r,r)\to(r,r+1)\to(r+1,r+1)\to\dots\to(2022,2023)\to(2023,2023)\to(2024,2023).$$
If it meets no monster, Turbo wins. Otherwise let the first monster met be at $(r,j)$; then $r\ge3$ and $j\in\{r,r+1\}$. *Attempt 3:*
$$(1,2)\to(2,2)\to(2,3)\to\dots\to(r-1,r-1)\to(r,r-1)\to(r,r-2)\to\dots\to(r,1)\to(r+1,1)\to\dots\to(2024,1).$$
The staircase part up to $(r-1,r-1)$ was passed safely in attempt 2; the cells $(r,c)$ with $c\le r-1$ are safe because row $r$'s monster is at $(r,j)$ with $j\ge r$; and column $1$ below row $2$ is safe because its only monster is at $(2,1)$. So attempt 3 succeeds.

**Answer: $n=3$.**

imo-2024-06.title: Injectivity and one clever substitution
imo-2024-06.body:
Write $x\to y$ if $f(x+f(y))=f(x)+y$. The second equation $f(f(x)+y)=x+f(y)$ says exactly $y\to x$, so for all $x,y$: $x\to y$ or $y\to x$. In particular $x\to x$, i.e. $f(x+f(x))=x+f(x)$.

**Example with two values ($c\ge2$).** Let $f(x)=\lfloor2x\rfloor-x$. For an integer $m$, $f(z+m)=f(z)+m$. Since $f(y)=\lfloor2y\rfloor-y$, we get $f(x+f(y))=f(x-y)+\lfloor 2y\rfloor$, so $x\to y$ iff $\lfloor2x-2y\rfloor+\lfloor2y\rfloor=\lfloor2x\rfloor$, i.e. iff $\{2x\}\ge\{2y\}$ (fractional parts). Similarly $y\to x$ iff $\{2y\}\ge\{2x\}$. One of these always holds, so $f$ is aquaesulian. Here $f(r)+f(-r)=\lfloor2r\rfloor+\lfloor-2r\rfloor$ is $0$ when $2r\in\mathbb Z$ and $-1$ otherwise: two values.

**$f$ is injective.** If $f(a)=f(b)$, say $a\to b$, then $f(a)+a=f(a+f(a))=f(a+f(b))=f(a)+b$, so $a=b$.

**Key claim.** If $s\to r$, then $f(r)+f(-r)=0$ or $f(f(s))=s+f(r)+f(-r)$.

*Proof.* Put $x=s+f(r)$ and $y=-r$. Then $f(x)=f(s+f(r))=f(s)+r$, so
$$x+f(y)=s+f(r)+f(-r),\qquad y+f(x)=f(s).$$
If $x\to y$: $f(s+f(r)+f(-r))=f(x)+y=f(s)$, so by injectivity $f(r)+f(-r)=0$. If $y\to x$: $f(f(s))=f(y+f(x))=f(y)+x=s+f(r)+f(-r)$. $\square$

**At most two values ($c\le2$).** Suppose $f(a)+f(-a)\ne0$ and $f(b)+f(-b)\ne0$. From $a\to a$ the claim gives $f(f(a))=a+f(a)+f(-a)$. Without loss of generality $a\to b$, and the claim gives $f(f(a))=a+f(b)+f(-b)$. Hence $f(a)+f(-a)=f(b)+f(-b)$: all nonzero values of $f(r)+f(-r)$ coincide, so there are at most two values in total ($0$ and one other).

**Answer:** the smallest $c$ is $2$.
